analysis.one_liner: Bans Medicare pharmacy middlemen from pocketing secret drug-price spreads and rebate-based fees.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan House committee approved the bill unanimously, 46 to 0, but House leaders never brought it to the floor for a vote before the two-year term ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs) are the middlemen that negotiate drug coverage for employers and Medicare plans. This bill would bar PBMs working for Medicare drug plans from making money on anything except flat-dollar service fees, stop them from charging plans more than they pay pharmacies (so-called spread pricing), stop them from paying their own pharmacies more than independent ones, and force them to disclose how much rebate money they keep instead of passing back to plans. It died in the House without ever getting a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries, who currently pay drug costs inflated by hidden PBM markups and rebate arrangements, and independent community pharmacies, which must compete against PBMs' own pharmacies on reimbursement rates the PBM itself sets.

how_it_helps.text: PBMs under Medicare drug-plan contracts could receive income only as flat-dollar service fees, not fees tied to drug prices or rebates, removing the incentive to prefer higher-priced drugs [S2].
PBMs could no longer charge a plan more for a drug's ingredient cost or dispensing fee than they actually reimburse the pharmacy, ending spread pricing in Medicare Part D [S2].

PBMs could not reimburse an affiliated pharmacy more than an independent network pharmacy for the same drug, protecting independent pharmacies from being undercut by their middleman's competitors [S2].
PBMs must report how much rebate and administrative-fee money they receive from drug manufacturers and how much they keep, and the government must publish the totals on a public website [S2].
PBMs would have to disgorge to the government any payments received in violation of the rules, and plans could suspend PBM payments for violations [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Pharmacy benefit managers and the large insurers that own them — CVS Caremark, Express Scripts (Cigna), and Optum Rx (UnitedHealth) — whose Medicare revenue depends on spread pricing, rebate-linked fees, and steering volume to affiliated pharmacies.
analysis.who_pays_short: PBM companies and their parent insurers

drawbacks.text: Banning rebate-based income could push PBMs to charge plans higher flat service fees, some of which may flow into premiums and plan costs; the bill caps the fee structure but not its level [S3].
The transparency provisions explicitly exempt trade secrets and confidential commercial information, so some PBM pricing practices could remain hidden [S3].
The bill covers only PBMs serving Medicare drug plans, leaving commercial-insurance patients under the same PBM practices [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits for Medicare patients and independent pharmacies are direct and the bill is narrowly drawn, but its biggest limitation is coverage: it only polices PBMs in Medicare Part D, not the much larger commercial market where the same practices operate, and its carve-outs for confidential information soften the transparency it promises.

outcome.mechanism: The House Energy and Commerce Committee unanimously approved the bill, but House leaders never scheduled it for a floor vote before the term ended, so it died without anyone voting on it.

narrative.text: Rep. Buddy Carter introduced the bill on April 26, 2023, with original cosponsors including Reps. Blunt Rochester, Malliotakis, and Auchincloss [S3].
It was sent to both the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees, and referred to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee [S5].
The Health Subcommittee forwarded the bill to the full committee by voice vote on November 15, 2023 [S5].
The full Energy and Commerce Committee ordered the bill reported, as amended, by a vote of 46 to 0 on December 6, 2023 [S5].
The bill never received a House floor vote; in December 2024 it was referred back to a subcommittee, and it died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5].
The bill had 45 cosponsors, split 26 Republicans and 19 Democrats [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmacy benefit managers and their parent insurers are better off, because they keep the spread-pricing and rebate-based revenue the bill would have banned in Medicare; Medicare beneficiaries keep paying the costs those practices add to drug prices.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: PBM companies and their parent insurers

for.name: Rep. Buddy Carter
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it through subcommittee and committee markup.

for.name: Reps. Blunt Rochester, Malliotakis, and Auchincloss
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction, giving the bill bipartisan sponsorship.

for.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
for.what_they_did: Approved the bill unanimously, 46 to 0, after subcommittee and full-committee markup sessions.

against.name: House majority leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a House floor vote despite its unanimous committee approval; it was instead referred back to a subcommittee in December 2024 and expired at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Major pharmacy benefit managers (CVS Caremark, Express Scripts, Optum Rx)
against.role: Industry — the three PBMs that manage prescription benefits for most Americans
against.what_they_did: Fought PBM regulation in Congress while the bill was pending; the bill would have banned their main Medicare revenue streams.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan at every stage: 45 cosponsors split 26 Republicans and 19 Democrats, and the committee voted 46 to 0 to advance the bill [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill bans the PBM business model's main revenue sources in Medicare: spread pricing, fees tied to drug prices and rebates, and payments received in violation of the rules must be disgorged [S2][S3]. PBMs profit by keeping the difference between what plans pay and what pharmacies receive, a cost built into Medicare drug prices for beneficiaries.

industries.industry: Vertically integrated insurers that own PBMs
industries.note: CVS (Aetna), Cigna, and UnitedHealth own the three largest PBMs, whose Medicare operations would lose spread and rebate income; the bill applies even when the PBM and plan sponsor are under common ownership [S2][S3].
The bill bars PBMs from reimbursing independent pharmacies less than their own affiliated pharmacies, ending a practice that pushes independent stores out of networks or into losses [S2].

Manufacturers currently pay PBMs large rebates for formulary placement; the bill requires PBMs to disclose rebates they keep rather than pass through, pressuring that arrangement, but leaves the rebate system itself in place [S2][S3].
